CITY OF THE GREAT, in the United States of North America, capital of the territory of Utah, in a beautiful and richly-cultivated plain, bounded on the E. by a range of snowy mountains bearing the name of Wasatchan, and on the W. by the Jordan River, on the right bank of which the city stands, about 22 miles S. of the Great Salt Lake, and 4350 feet above the level of the

SALTASH

Pages 596-596

a market-town of England, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cornwall, 34 miles N.W. of Davenport. The houses rise tier above tier on the steep <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tamar, and present striking and picturesque contrasts; some being of brick, some of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, some fronted with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, others with slates. There is a town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, an old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school. Most of the inhabitants are fishermen. Saltash was formerly a parliamentary burgh, returning two members, but was disfranchised by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-REFORM">Reform</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">Act</a> of 1832. Pop. 1621.

SALTOATS

Pages 596-596

a seaport-town of Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AYR">Ayr</a>, 24 miles S.W. of Glasgow. It is built on the shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of Ayr, and has some good houses, but it is in general a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>-looking <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. There is a town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a> with an elegant spire, an Established <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a Free church, two belonging to the United <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, and one to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. The inhabitants are supported chiefly by the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> and sewing of muslin for the Glasgow market. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> is manufactured, and at either end of the town there are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> chemical works. Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which formerly formed an important branch of the industry of the place, has of late years much declined. Large quantities of coals are exported to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. The harbour however is not good, and inferior to that of Ardrossan. Pop. 4338.

SALVAGE

Pages 597-597

an allowance made to those persons, other than the crew, by whom ships <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> goods have been saved from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, fire, pirates, or enemies. 1. In fixing the rate of salvage upon losses by perils at sea, regard is usually had, not only to the labour and peril incurred by the salvors, but also to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of relationship to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> saved, the anxiety manifested by them, the value of the ship and cargo, and the danger from which they were rescued. Sometimes a half, sometimes a tenth of the property saved has gone to the salvors. 2. During a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, when British war-ships re-capture British merchantmen from the enemy, they are allowed a salvage of one-eighth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the re-captured ships and cargoes (stat. 43 Geo. III., c. 160), and one-sixth part of their value on ships re-captured by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a>. An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of her Majesty's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> (16 and 17 Vict., c. 131) lays <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> several regulations regarding Salvandy the prosecution of such claims. (For further information regarding salvage, see the works of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBOT">Abbot</a>, and of Maude and Pollock, on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a> of Shipping; and McCulloch's Commercial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>.)

SALVANDY

Pages 597-597

Narcisse Achille, Comte de, a French writer and statesman, sprung from an Irish family, was born at Condom, in the department of Gers, on the 11th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1796. Having been sent at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he received his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the Lycée Napoléon. The needy youth enrolled himself in a volunteer corps in 1812, and served with much distinction throughout the campaigns of 1813-14, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to receive the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> of the Legion of Honour from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> on the 6th of April 1814. On the restoration of the Bourbons, Salvandy expressed his devotedness to the new regime in these words: "After having shed my blood in an illegitimate cause," he wrote to the Duc d'Angoulême, "I would die for the Bourbons." Having accompanied <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XVIII. to the Belgian frontier in 1815, he returned to Paris, and published his pamphlets, Mémoire sur les Griefs et les Vœux de la France; and Observations sur le Champ de Mai. Next year he brought out La Coalition et la France, which produced a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> in the courts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In 1819 he was made a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of State, and appointed Maître des Requêtes; but the French cabinet not acting according to his liking in the electoral system, he had the audacity, at the risk of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, to defend that system in his clever brochures Vues Politiques and Dangers de la Situation présente. In 1820, Salvandy having gone to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> during the ministry of the Duc de Richelieu, studied with warm <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> the liberal movement in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In 1823 appeared his celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a> Alonso, ou l'Espagne, which has been frequently reprinted. In 1824 began his connection with the Journal des Débats, which was destined to continue at intervals for the next twenty years. In his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> he pursued a bold yet steady course, scorning to fawn upon any potentate, and flattering no party. He never abandoned his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> principle, that there was no security for France but in constitutional <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>—a maxim which he urged with all the warmth of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and energy of style competent to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a lively imagination and of perfect self-consciousness. Salvandy held the position of councillor of state during the ministry of Martignac, but resigned on the subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the cabinet. During the reign of Louis Philippe, he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to pursue his liberal policy, both in political leader and in pamphlet, with the same steady adherence which had hitherto characterised him. He held several offices of state, was made a member of the French Academy, and was created a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a>. On the coup d'état of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1851, he went into retirement, and died on the 15th December 1856, in his sixty-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year.

SALWEEN

Pages 597-597
or Salleen, a large river of Further India, rises on the eastern frontiers of Tibet, and flows southwards, forming, for a great part of its course, the eastern boundary of Burmah, and then entering the British dominions, and separating Pegu from the Tenasserim provinces. It falls into the Gulf of Mastaban by a broad mouth, between the towns of Moulenin and Mastaban. The whole length is estimated at 600 miles; and though the river has been very little explored, it is believed to flow through a fertile, well-wooded country, and to be navigable for a considerable distance from the sea.

SALZBURG

Pages 597-599
Duchy of, a crown-land of the Austrian empire, bounded on the N. and N.E. by Upper Austria, E. by Upper Austria and Styria, S. by Carinthia and the Tyrol, and W. by the Tyrol and Bavaria; area, 2757 square miles. It is almost entirely mountainous, being occupied by that chain of the Alps called the Salzburg Salzburg, Alps or the Tasern. These extend along the southern frontier, and send off many branches, forming glens and valleys of exquisite romantic beauty. The principal summits are the Wiesbach or Krummborn, 11,297 feet high; and the Kitzsteinhorn, 10,106 feet. The Salzach rises on the borders of Tyrol, and flows at first eastwards down the romantic valley called Pinzgau; then turns suddenly to the north, and traversing the equally fine valley called by its name, leaves Salzburg to join the Inn on the frontiers of Bavaria and Upper Austria. Almost all the rivers of the country discharge their waters into this, which is by far the most important. There are a number of lakes and many exceedingly beautiful waterfalls in Salzburg. Notwithstanding the mountainous nature of the surface, the valleys are in general very fertile, and a large proportion of the soil is productive. Corn is raised in considerable quantities, and excellent vegetables may be grown in sheltered spots; but it is the rearing of cattle that forms the chief support of the inhabitants. Of minerals, gold, silver, copper, lead, iron, manganese, and arsenic are obtained; salt, too, is extensively worked, especially in the great salt-works at Hallein. In many places there are mineral springs. The manufacturing industry of the country is, on the whole, not very highly developed. The present duchy of Salzburg was formerly an archbishopric, immediately dependent on the German empire. Christianity was introduced here among the heathen inhabitants by a Scotishman named Rupert, afterwards canonized, who found the land nearly a desert, and became the first bishop of Salzburg in 716. The see was afterwards raised to the rank of an archbishopric, and its occupant became primate of Germany, and was the only archbishop, besides the spiritual electors, who had a seat and voice in the diet. The privileges of these prelates were numerous; their temporal possessions gradually became extensive, and their revenues enormous. The Reformed doctrines early found admission into Salzburg, but the utmost severity was used to suppress them, until at last, in 1732, the Protestant states obtained leave for their fellow Protestants to leave the country, on which more than 30,000 departed, and settled in Prussia, Württemberg, and in the North American colony of Georgia. In 1801 the see was secularized, and given to the ex-Duke of Tuscany, with the title of Elector; but by the peace of Pressburg in 1806, it was annexed to Austria. From 1809 to 1815 Salzburg belonged to Bavaria; but in the latter year, with the exception of a small portion, it was restored to Austria. The inhabitants are almost all Germans, and of the Roman Catholic religion. Pop. (1854) 154,379. Salzburg, the capital of the above duchy, on both sides of the Salzach or Salza, just at the entrance of the hill country, where the river issues from its confined valley into the Bavarian plain, 156 miles W.S.W. of Vienna. Few German towns can rival this in the beauty of its situation: the stream, with greyish-white water, telling of distant glaciers, flows among meadows and waving corn-fields, between two castle-crowned cliffs, at the foot of which clusters the Italian-like town, with its flat roofs, numerous churches, and marble edifices; while in the background rise the slopes of hills darkly clothed in wood, and the scene is closed in by the snowy line of loftier mountains in the remote distance. The part of the town that lies to the left of the river is almost inclosed by the Castle Hill (Schlossberg) and the Monk's Hill (Mönchberg); while a bridge 370 feet long leads to the other portion, on the slope of the Capuchin Hill (Capuzinerberg). On the summits of the two latter hills there are extensive plateaus, laid out in fine walks, and planted with trees. The ancient castle on the hill, to which it gives its name, has been long dismantled, and is now only used for barracks. Its towers rise 400 feet above the square below. Besides the natural strength of its position, Salzburg is defended by fortifications, and entered by eight gates. One of the latter, called the New Gate, is formed by a tunnel cut through the Monk's Hill, constructed by Archbishop Sigismund in 1767. The cathedral is a large and splendid marble edifice in the Italian style, built in the seventeenth century. Near it is the former archbishop's palace, now occupied by public offices. In the square in front stands a beautiful marble fountain and a statue of Mozart, who was born here in a house that is still to be seen marked with an inscription. Among the many churches of the town, that of St Peter is remarkable for its monuments, and for a curious old churchyard attached to it. There are numerous convents, one of which, the Benedictine, is among the oldest in Germany, and has a fine library. The Lyceum, formerly a university, has also a library of 36,000 volumes and 300 MSS. There are other schools, a theatre, several hospitals, &c., in the town. The manufactures comprise leather, iron wire, and pottery; the trade is considerable; and two annual markets are held. Salzburg is still the seat of an archbishop; also of the provincial government and courts of law. Pop. (1851), exclusive of the military, 17,009. Samakov, a town of European Turkey, Bulgaria, at the foot of the north slope of the Balkan hills, in the Sandjak, and 30 miles S.E. of Sophia. It is defended by an embattled wall, flanked with towers; and has manufactures of heavy iron goods, the materials for which are obtained from the mines in the vicinity. Pop. 5000. Samar, one of the Philippine s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands, lying to the S.E. of Luzon, separated from it by a strait 20 miles wide, between N. Lat. 11. and 12. 48., E. Long. 24. 25. and 25. 55. Its form is triangular, with the apex pointing southwards; length, 150 miles; greatest breadth, 80; area, 5470 square miles. The northern portion is occupied by rugged, lofty mountains; while the whole is densely wooded, and watered by numerous rivers, large and small. The climate is healthy, the soil moderately fertile, and the productions numerous, including many useful and valuable woods, palm oil, cocoas, rice, Manila hemp, &c. Samar is inhabited by a mixed race, the offspring of Spaniards by Indian mothers; they manufacture mats and other articles, and carry on some trade. The island belongs to Spain; and the capital is Cabalunger, on the west coast. Pop. 99,635. Samara, a government of European Russia, bounded on the N. by that of Kasan, E. by Orenburg and the Kirghizee territory, S. by Astrakhan, and W. by Saratov and Simbirsk; area, 51,588 square miles. It consists of a broad, open, slightly undulating plain, lying between the rivers Volga and Ural,—the former of which bounds the government on the west, and the latter on the east. By these rivers and their affluents, especially those of the Volga, the country is watered. The government was formed by an ukase in December 1850, from portions of those of Orenburg, Saratov, and Simbirsk, in the following proportions:— | From Orenburg, 3 districts | 21,293 | |---------------------------|--------| | Saratov, parts of 2 districts | 20,102 | | Simbirsk, 2 districts | 10,093 | Total | 51,588 | Thus, in the statistics given of these governments for 1849, those parts are included which now belong to Samara, as the new government had not then been formed. The great majority of the inhabitants belong to the Greek Church; but there were also, in 1851, 122,113 Mohammedans, 48,583 Protestants, 32,140 Roman Catholics, 3426 pagans, and a few Jews. The government is divided into seven circles, as follows:— | Pop. (1850) | Pop. (1851) | |-------------|-------------| | Samara | 146,293 | | Stavropol | 163,534 | | Nicolaevsk | 250,585 | | Novyi Usen | 133,984 | | Buguruslan | 221,322 | | Bagulma | 146,880 | | Basulak | 257,210 | Total | 1,320,108 | Samara. SAMARA, the capital of the above government, at the confluence of the river of the same name with the Volga, 550 miles E.S.E. of Moscow. It was originally built in 1591 as a defence against the incursions of the Bashkirs and the Kalmyks, and for that purpose was surrounded by an earthen wall and a deep moat. These fortifications were destroyed in 1703, and a citadel built in their stead, but of this only a few vestiges are now to be seen. The town contains two cathedrals and three other churches, a gymnasium and various other schools, several charitable institutions, cloth and silk factories, &c. Near the confluence of the rivers is a double row of warehouses built of pine wood, and supported by tarred pillars. These, as well as others in different parts of the town, are used in connection with the great fairs held here twice a year,—one in the second week of Lent, and the other on the 14th (26th) September. Each of the warehouses can contain from 25,000 to 30,000 cwt. of corn. For a long time Samara has been one of the principal markets for corn on the Volga; and in 1852 there were sold here 631,412 quarters of wheat, and 16,613 of linseed. The value of goods brought to the first fair is generally about £41,000, of which £13,000 worth are sold; that of those brought to the second about £66,000, of which £20,000 worth are sold. Pop. 24,405.

SAMARANG

Pages 599-599

a seaport of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a Dutch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, at the mouth of a river of the same name, on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, 240 E.S.E. of Batavia. It is pretty well built, and encircled with a wall and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>, sufficiently strong to resist any attacks of the natives. The river forms a harbour, which is rather shallow; but about 2 miles off there is a roadstead commanded by a fort. There are here a Protestant and a Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, several mosques, a school, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">Leather</a> and cotton fabrics are manufactured, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> trade with the interior is carried on, coffee, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a> being exported. Pop. about 50,000.

SAMARCAND

Pages 599-599

a fortified <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Turkestan, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> and 100 miles east of Bokhara, in the midst of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> exceedingly beautiful and fertile, on the Soyd <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Zer Afshan, once the splendid seat of the triumphs of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TAMERLANE">Tamerlane</a>, and inhabited then by 150,000 people. It is now in a very decayed condition, and many of its former streets are covered with ruins, or occupied by fields, gardens, or groves. The most conspicuous and interesting <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> of Tamerlane and his family, a magnificently-ornamented octagonal building, surmounted by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOME">dome</a>. In the citadel stands the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the Emir or Khan of Bokhara. Under Tamerlane, Samarcan was a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> seat of Mohammedan learning, and contained no less than forty medresses or colleges; but of these, three only remain,—<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> buildings with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> mosaic on the walls and minarets at the corners. Of the numerous mosques, too, many are quite in ruins. The only important <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> buildings are the bazaar and caravansaries. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> of cotton and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a> cloth, silk <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> are carried on. The trade of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has much declined, having been nearly all transferred to Bokhara, and comparatively little business is now done except when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> from various <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> visit the town. Pop. about 10,000. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAMARIA">SAMARIA</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PALESTINE">PALESTINE</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SAMARITANS">SAMARITANS</a>. In the books of Kings there are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> notices of the origin of the people called Samaritans. The ten tribes which revolted from Rehoboam, son of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, chose Jeroboam for their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>. After his elevation to the throne he set up <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> calves at Dan and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BETHEL">Bethel</a>, lest repeated visits of his subjects to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, for the purpose of worshipping the true God, should withdraw their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> from himself. Afterwards Samaria, built by Omri, became the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of Israel, and thus the separation between Judah and Israel was rendered complete. The people took the name Samaritans from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city. In the ninth year of Hosea, Samaria was taken by the Assyrians under Shalmaneser, who carried away the inhabitants into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, and introduced colonies into their place. The dregs of the populace, particularly those who appeared incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, were not taken away by the victors. With them, therefore, the heathen colonists became incorporated. But the latter were far more numerous than the former, and had all power in their own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The remnant of the Israelites was so inconsiderable and insignificant as not to affect, to any important <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, the opinions of the new inhabitants. As the people were a mixed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>, their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> also assumed a mixed character. In it the worship of idols was associated with that of the true God. But apostacy from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JEHOVAH">Jehovah</a> was not universal. On the return of the Jews from the Babylonish captivity, the Samaritans wished to join them in rebuilding the Temple, saying, "Let us build with you; for we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esarhaddon, king of Assur, which brought us up hither" (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> iv. 2). But the Jews declined the proffered assistance; and from this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Samaritans threw every obstacle in their way. Hence arose that inveterate enmity between the two nations which afterwards increased to such a height as to become proverbial. In the reign of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Nothus, Manasses, son of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, married the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANBALLAT">Sanballat</a> the Samaritan governor; and to avoid the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of repudiating her, as the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Moses required, went over to the Samaritans, and became high-priest in the temple which his father-in-law built for him on Mount Gerizim. From this time Samaria became a refuge for all malcontent Jews; and the very name of each people became odious to the other. About the year B.C. 109 John Hyrcanus, high-priest of the Jews, destroyed the city and temple of the Samaritans; but Herod rebuilt them at great expense B.C. 25. In their new temple, however, the Samaritans could not be induced to offer sacrifices, but still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to worship on Gerizim. At the present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> they have dwindled <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to a few families. Shechem, now called Nablus, is their place of abode. They still possess a copy of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic law</a>. A different account of the origin of this people has been given by Hengstenberg, whom Havermick and Robinson follow. It has been ably combated by Kalkar (in Pelz's Mitarbeiten for 1840, drittes Heft, p. 24, &c.), to whom the reader is referred. With the remnant above referred to, a correspondence was formerly maintained by several learned Europeans, but without leading to any important result. It was commenced by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger in 1559; and resumed, after a century, by several learned men in England in 1675, and by the great Ethiopic scholar, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JOB">Job</a> Ludolf, in 1684. The illustrious orientalist De Sacy also held correspondence with them. All their letters to England and France, and all that was then known respecting them, he published in a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled, "Correspondance des Samaritains," &c., in Notices et Extraits des MSS. de la Bibliotheque du Roi, tom. xii. The best accounts of them given by modern travellers are by Pliny Fisk (American Missionary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERALD">Herald</a> for 1824), who visited them in 1823; and by Robinson and Smith, who visited them in 1838 (see Biblical Researches and Travels in Palestine, iii. 113-116).

SAMARRAH

Pages 599-600

a town of Asiatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, on a cliff forming the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tigris, in the paschalic and 65 miles N.N.W. of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>. It is a miserable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, encircled by a wall, and only remarkable for two beautiful monuments to Moslem saints, both surmounted by domes, one of which, once covered with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, is now quite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; while the other is beautifully enamelled with white and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on a bluish ground. These attract pilgrims from all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 10,000 yearly; but the resident <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> does not exceed 1000.

SAMBAS

Pages 600-600

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BORNEO">Borneo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a Mohammedan state of the same name, on the River Sambas, about 30 miles from its mouth, on the west <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, 72 miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Pontianak. It lies in a low, swampy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and the houses are generally raised on piles. There is here the residence of a native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, tributary to the Dutch, and of a Dutch resident. Pop. 9400. The country is fertile and populous, and contains the richest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in Borneo. These are worked by Chinese. The River Sambas flows generally west, and after a course of 100 miles, falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Ocean. It is navigable for boats as far as Sambas, and has auriferous sands.

SAMBOR

Pages 600-600

a town of the Austrian empire, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a circle of the same name in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, on the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Dniester, 46 miles S.W. of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEMBERG">Lemberg</a>. It contains an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Bernardine convent, a gymnasium and normal school, courts of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">Linen</a> cloth is manufactured here; and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> trade is carried on. Pop. 10,682.

SAMNIUM

Pages 600-600

one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> districts of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Central <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. The name was sometimes used in a more extensive, sometimes in a more restricted <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. In the more usual sense of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a>, Samnium was an inland district, bounded on the N. by the Mursi, Peligni, and Frentani, E. by Apulia, S. by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>, S.W. and W. by Campanium and Latium. The Samnites were a people of Sabine origin, who migrated into this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> at a comparatively late <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> either of their earlier <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> later <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> is unknown. They became finally swallowed up by the Roman people, after having engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of desperate struggles known as the Samnite Wars. (See <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>.)

SAMOS

Pages 600-600

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Grecian Archipelago, lying off the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, from which it is separated by the strait of Little Boghaz, where narrowest, not more than a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> wide. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Boghaz, which is about 10 miles in width, separates the other extremity of the island from Icaria. Samos is about 27 miles in length from E. to W., by about 12 in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> breadth; and is between 37° 35' and 37° 48' N. Lat., and 26° 36' and 27° 8' E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. It is elevated and mountainous, being traversed by two lofty ranges of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> stretching from E. to W.; but there are also many valleys of considerable size, especially towards the south. The highest summit, called Kerkeis, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Cercetus Mons, reaches the height of 4725 feet, and is covered with perpetual snow. The mountains are in some places steep and barren; but for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> they are at present, as in the times of antiquity, covered with forests of oaks and pines, with vineyards, and with olive-grounds. A few small <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> the island, and some traces have been discovered of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRRIGATION">irrigation</a>. The rocks consist mainly of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, which is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mineral production. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">Iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and silver are also obtained. In the valleys the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very rich, and the scenery beautiful. Celebrated in ancient times for its great fertility, Samos is still one of the most productive <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Archipelago, though it has not now the advantage of that careful system of cultivation which made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all the available ground by means of terraces along the mountain-sides. Corn, wine, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, figs, cotton, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a> are the principal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of export. The Samian wine, which is now much esteemed, did not enjoy a favourable reputation in the ancient world. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town in the island is Chora <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Khora, which stands near the site of Samos, the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 1000. It is defended by a castle, and has a good harbour. There are other small ports on different parts of the coast. Samos now belongs to the Turkish empire; but has enjoyed since 1835 a position of virtual independence, governed by a Greek with the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of Samos," and paying a fixed annual tribute to the Porte. In the earliest times the island bore several names besides the one which it ultimately retained, and which was given to it most probably on account of its elevated character. The original inhabitants are said to have been Carians and Leleges; but at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a> to Asia, Greek settlers established themselves, and Samos became an important member of the Ionian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>. It was chiefly distinguished for commercial and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> enterprise: its ships exhibited the earliest improvements in naval <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; and one of its citizens was the first who passed the pillars of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, and visited Tartessus. Several colonies were founded by Samos on the shores of the Ægean and the Propontis. During the short but prosperous reign of Polycrates (B.C. 532-522), the Samian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> was the most powerful in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and the island maintained its independence of the Persian empire, being in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> at first with Amasis of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and afterwards with his enemy Cambyses of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. The capital was at that time one of the finest cities in the world, and was encircled by many public works and buildings constructed by the monarch. He resided in a fortified <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; there was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> Ionic temple of Juno by a native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, a harbour inclosed by two artificial moles, and a tunnel hewn out of the rock to convey water to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. At this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, too, Samos was distinguished as the birth-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>; and Anacreon resided for some time at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Polycrates. The reign of that monarch, however, came to a disastrous end in 522, when he was treacherously put to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by a Persian satrap. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> then appointed Syloson, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Polycrates, to succeed him; but he could only be placed on the throne after a general massacre, which almost reduced the island to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. Samos was now virtually subject to Persia, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be so, with a short <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> at the time of the Ionian revolt, until the victory of the Greeks at Mycale, B.C. 479, obtained its freedom. It then became a member of the Athenian confederacy; but after a time revolted, and was in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> reduced to complete subjection by the Athenians. This happened in 439, and from that period till 412 Samos had neither a fleet nor any fortifications; but at the latter <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> it became a place of importance, and was the head-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the Athenian fleet in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> contest with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>. After this time few historical events are connected with Samos. It was celebrated for its school of statuary; and under the Roman empire was a free city, while the temple of Juno enjoyed the privileges of a sanctuary. It is unnecessary to enter minutely into the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Samos during the middle ages, during which, after having been held for a long time by the Arabs, it was recovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Leo in the thirteenth century, and then successively fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Venetians, Genoese, and Turks. At the time of the Greek insurrection the Samians zealously embraced the side of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. They expelled the Turks from the island, which they put into a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, establishing an independent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Various attempts were made by the Turks to regain the island, but they were all foiled by the courage of the people and the vigilance of the Greek fleet. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, however, which secured the independence and defined the limits of Greece, Samos was still left to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, and the subsequent efforts that she has made have only secured a partial freedom. The ancient remains in the island are very inconsiderable; they are all near the site of the capital, towards the S.W., and consist chiefly of some fragments of the city walls, some traces of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, a single <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of the great temple, and the moles of the harbour. The present population of Samos is estimated at 50,000.

SAMOTHRACE

Pages 600-601

called by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Greeks Samothraki, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Ægean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, about 38 miles S. of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Thrace, and 40 N.W. of the mouth of the Hellespont. It is oval in form, about 8 miles in length by Samothrace is 6 in breadth, and has an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 30 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It is very lofty, the highest point, Mount Fingaree (anciently called Sace), being the most conspicuous object, next to Mount <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHOS">Athos</a>, in this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the sea, and, except Mount Ida in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, the most elevated point in the whole Archipelago. Hence it is represented by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> as the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> when viewing the plains of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; and modern travellers have confirmed the accuracy of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> by observing from these plains the island towering up over the low intervening surface of Imbros. Corn, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and wax are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> productions of the island. It has no good harbours, but some anchorages on its coast. Samothrace was chiefly celebrated in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times as the seat of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the Cabiri, into which many celebrated men were initiated. No important event, either in ancient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> in modern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is connected with the island. Pop. about 15,000, partly Greeks and partly Turks.

SAMOYEDES

Pages 601-601

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> of people in the Russian empire, occupying the shores of the Arctic Ocean, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of Kamin, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Archangel, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of Katanska, in the N.E. of that of Yenisieisk. Properly speaking, they are a branch of the Finnic race, but are so widely distinguished from that race that they may be considered a separate one. They are divided into three parts,—Samoyedes of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, inhabiting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> E. of the Petchora; those of the Little Land, farther west; and those of the Kamin peninsula, the most westerly of all. Their numbers are not great, and they <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a wandering <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, subsisting chiefly by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>.

SAMSOON

Pages 601-601

a seaport-town of Asiatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, pashalic of Sivas, on the shore of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, 166 miles W.N.W. of Trebizond. It has mosques, khans, and a small bazaar; and is chiefly remarkable as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of trade, whence the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, wheat, &c., of the surrounding <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> are conveyed to Constantinople. The commercial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of the place received a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> impulse during the Crimean <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, on the opposite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Black Sea; but after the peace it relapsed into its old state, and the difficulty of internal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> prevents any permanent advance. Pop. 2000. SAMUEL. (See SAMUEL, BOOKS OF.)

SAMUEL

Pages 601-602

BOOKS OF. The two books of Samuel were anciently reckoned as but one among the Jews. That they form only one treatise is apparent from their structure. The present <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> into two books, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> Bibles since the editions of Bomberg, was derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> and Vulgate, in both which versions they are termed the First and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Books of Kings. Thus <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> (apud Euseb. Hist. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLES">Eccles</a>. vi. 25), in his famous catalogue of the Hebrew Scriptures, names the books of Samuel; so also does Jerome. It was desirable to have short names for the books of Scripture; and as Samuel was a prophet of such celebrity, and had such influence in changing the form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> under which the son of Kish and the son of Jesse became sovereigns, it was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to name after him the biographical tracts in which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and times of these <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> chieftains are briefly sketched, especially as they at the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> contain striking descriptions of the miracle of his own birth, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> of his youth, and the impressive actions of his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. The selection of this Jewish name might also be strengthened by the national <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the authorship of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, founded on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of 1 Chron. xxix. 29. The contents of the books of Samuel belong to an interesting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. The first book of Samuel gives an account of the birth and early call of that prophet to the duties of a seer under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELI">Eli</a>'s pontificate; describes the low and degraded condition of the people, oppressed by foreign enemies; proceeds to narrate the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of Samuel as judge; his prosperous regency; the degeneracy of his sons; the clamour for a change in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; the installation of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>; his rash and reckless character; his neglect of, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> opposition to, the theocratic elements of the government. Then the historian goes on to relate God's choice of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>; his endurance of long and harassing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> from the reigning sovereign; the melancholy defeat and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Saul on the field of Gilboa; the gradual elevation of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> "according to God's own heart" to universal dominion; his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> efforts to obey and follow out the principles of the theocracy; his formal establishment of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, now the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of victories over all the enemies of Judah that were wont to molest its frontiers. The annalist records David's aberrations from the path of duty; the unnatural rebellion of his son Absalom, and its suppression; his carrying into effect a census of his dominions, and the Divine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> which this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> incurred; and concludes with a few characteristic sketches of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>. The second book of Samuel, while it relates the last words of David, yet stops short of his death. As David was the real founder of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> and arranger of the religious economy; the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, and poet of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; as his dynasty maintained itself on the throne of Judah till the Babylonian invasion; it is not a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of wonder that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of his life and government occupies so large a portion of early Jewish history. The books of Samuel thus consist of three interlaced biographies,—those of Samuel, Saul, and David. The attempt to ascertain the authorship of this early history is attended with difficulty. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is in favour of the usual <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>, that the first twenty-four chapters were written by Samuel, and the rest by Nathan and Gad. Abarbanel, however, and Grotius, suppose Jeremiah to be the author (Grot. Prof. in 1 Sam.). The peculiar theory of Jahn is, that the four books of Samuel and Kings were written by the same person, and at a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> so recent as the thirteenth year of the Babylonish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. His arguments, however, are more ingenious than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> (Introduction, Turner's Translation, § 46). The fact of all the four treatises being named Books of Kings, Jahn insists upon as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that they were originally undivided and formed a single work—a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, since the similarity of their contents might easily give rise to this general <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, while the more ancient appellation for the first two was The Books of Samuel. Jahn also lays great stress on the uniformity of method in all the books. But this uniformity by no means amounts to any proof of identity of authorship. It is nothing more than the same Hebrew historical style. The more minute and distinctive features, so far from being similar, are very different. The books of Samuel and Kings may be contrasted in many of those peculiarities which mark a different writer. The books of Samuel have an authorship of their own—an authorship belonging to a very early period. While their tone and style are very different from the later records of Chronicles, they are also dissimilar to the books of Kings. They bear the impress of a hoary <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> in their language, allusions, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. The insertion of odes and snatches of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, to enliven and verify the narrative, is common to them with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>. The minute sketches and vivid touches with which they abound prove that their author "speaks what he knows, and testifies what he has seen." As <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the chapters had been extracted from a diary, some portions are more fully detailed and warmly coloured than others, according as the observer was himself impressed. From public and acknowledged sources has the compiler fetched his materials, in the shape of connected excerpts. The last of the prophetic triumvirate might be the redactor or editor of the work, and we would not date its publication later than the death of Nathan, while the original biographies may have been finished at the period of David's decease. But certainty on such a subject is not to be attained. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PROBABILITY">Probability</a> is all that we dare assert. The compiler has in all probability framed out of authoritative documents a consecutive history, not dwelling on all events with equal <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, but passing slightly over some, and formally detailing others with national relish and delight. Credibility The authenticity of the history found in the books of Samuel rests on sufficient grounds. Portions of them are quoted in the New <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> (2 Sam. vii. 14, in Heb. i. 5; 1 Sam. xiii. 14, in Acts xiii. 22). References to them occur in other sections of Scripture, especially in the Psalms, to which they often afford historic illustration. It has been argued against them that they contain contradictory statements. The old objections of Hobbes, Spinoza, Simon, and Le Clerc are well disposed of by Carpzovius (Introductio, p. 218). Some of these supposed contradictions we have already referred to; and for a solution of others, especially of seeming <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> between the books of Samuel and Chronicles, we refer with satisfaction to Davidson's Sacred Hermeneutics, p. 544, &c. Some of the objections of Vatke, in his Bibl. Theol., are summarily disposed of by Hengstenberg (Die Authentie des Pentateu., vol. ii., p. 115), who usually chastises such adversaries with a whip of scorpions. Discrepancies in numbers, and sometimes in proper names, are the most common; and it is well known that textual errors in numeration are both most frequently and most easily committed. Victorini Strigelii Comm. in quatuor Libr. Reg. et Paralipp., 1624, folio; N. Serrarii Comm. in lib. Josuex Jud., Ruth, Reg., et Paralipp., 1609, folio; Seb. Schmidt, In Lib. Sam. Comm., 1684-89, 4to; Jac. Bonfrenii Comm. in lib. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUART">quart</a>. Reg., &c., 1643; Clerici Comm. in lib. Sam.; <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a>, T. ii.; Jo. Drusii Annotat. in Locos diffic. Jos., Jud., Sam., 1618; Hensler, Erläuterungen des I. B. Sam. &c., 1795; Maurer, Comment. Critic. p. 1; Exegetische Handbuch des A. T., st. iv. v.; Chandler's Critical History of the Life of David, 2 vols., 1786. SANÀ, a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, the capital of Yemen or Arabia Felix, 4000 feet above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in a beautiful valley extending from N. to S., from 6 to 9 miles <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and bounded on either side by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-lands, 110 miles N.N.E. of Hodeda; N. Lat. 15.22, E. Long. 44.31. The streets are in general narrow, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> one is crossed by a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, as in rainy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> a stream of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> runs through it. The houses are large, and those of the upper classes have windows filled with fine stained glass. A wall, about 5½ miles in circuit, surrounds the town, and has a few gates; but it is in a very ruinous condition. There are about 20 mosques, in general very splendid, and many of them surmounted by gilt domes. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol16.html#article-SANA">Sana</a> also has a bazaar, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> similar to those of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. But the principal buildings are the two large palaces of the imam, which have extensive gardens attached to them, the whole being surrounded with fortifications. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of these edifices is Saracenic, with an intermixture of round and pointed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, but they are devoid of all superfluous ornaments. Most of the artisans in Sana are Jews, who live in a separate <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the town, and are subject to much oppression, paying heavy taxes for permission to reside in the town, and for the possession of gardens or vineyards. They, as well as the Banians, who form a large proportion of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, are obliged to conceal their wealth, and they live by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of jewellery, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, spirits, &c. The most important and wealthy class in Sana are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. The principal article of export is the coffee grown in the vicinity; while <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, thread, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, velvet, glass, dates, spices, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, &c., are imported. Sana has been governed by an imam ever since the Turks were expelled from this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Arabia, in the reign of Soliman the Magnificent. Some ancient <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> have been discovered here. Pop. about 40,000.

SAN FELIPE

Pages 606-606

a town of Venezuela, in the department of Caracas, near the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Yuracuy, 60 San Felipe miles W.N.W. of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>. It is well built, but lies in a low, unhealthy region, liable to inundations. Coffee, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CACAO">cacao</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a> are produced here, and there is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> trade. Pop. 7000.

SAN FELIPE DE ACONCAGUA

Pages 606-606
capital of the province of Aconcagua in Chili, on the right bank of the river of the same name, 40 miles north of Santiago. It is well built, and is considered one of the finest towns in the interior. There are here three convents, and in the vicinity copper and gold mines. Pop. 8000.

SAN FRANCISCO

Pages 606-607

the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commercial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALIFORNIA">California</a>, in the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, at the mouth of the splendid <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of San Francisco, through which the river Sacramento issues into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, N. Lat. 37.48., W. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 122.26. It occupies the northern extremity of a tongue of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> that encloses the bay on the west; and its site consists of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plain, gently sloping from the hills behind <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the bay. The city was originally built round a semi-circular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> facing the north-east, but this is now covered with warehouses erected on piles, and the rapidly increasing buildings are extending backwards from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> and climbing the hills behind, which are only about half a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from the shore. From <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TELEGRAPH">Telegraph</a> Hill to the north, a magnificent view is obtained over the city and surrounding <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. To the west lies the ocean and the entrance of the bay; to the north its northern arm, leading up the Sacramento river, and ever studded with steamers; to the east, beyond the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> sheet of water, a panorama of wooded hills, with the cone of Monte Diablo in the distance; and to the south the city itself, with its perpetual bustle and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, its wharves crowded with shipping from all parts of the world. The streets are all regularly laid out, crossing one another at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>; but the buildings exhibit the utmost variety in the form and materials of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, though brick is now beginning to be most generally used. Some of the public buildings, such as the churches, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, &c., are equal to any in the United States; and many of the hotels and shops are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and splendid. But the rapidity of the changes that come over the appearance of San Francisco renders it vain to give any detailed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Many important <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are carried on in the town. There are two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-houses, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> mill, two <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> factories, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-works, and shipbuilding yards; while agricultural implements, furniture, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, tubs, pails, musical instruments, &c., are also made here. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, especially its recent rapid rise, is not a little remarkable. Its original name was Yerba Buena, and it first rose in connection with one of the Spanish mission settlements, called San Francisco, founded in 1776. From that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> till 1831 the settlement <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to flourish under the Spanish, and latterly under the Mexican, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; but the disturbances which then agitated the country drove away the Indians, and reduced the settlement to ruins. A new city was founded in 1839, but the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1845 did not exceed 150. Numerous settlers from the United States began to flock hither, even before California was ceded to that country in 1848. But in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> of the previous year a new era opened for San Francisco with the discovery of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. No sooner was the fact generally known, in the next <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, than the city was almost deserted for the diggings; trade was at an end, and all business seemed to have ceased. But this did not last long, for in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of August eager crowds of emigrants began to arrive, the harbour was thronged with ships, and the city far more than before alive with bustle and din. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a> was soon commenced with vigour, the value of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> rose rapidly, and in little more than a year the population had risen to more than 15,000. De- San Francisco's fires broke out on several occasions, and laid large portions of the city in ashes; but these injuries were speedily repaired. By these calamities, as well as by a reckless expenditure, the financial affairs of the city were reduced to a very low state; but by the imposition of heavy taxes the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> was restored from a state of almost hopeless bankruptcy. So much gold poured into the town as to render it necessary in 1853 to establish a mint in San Francisco. The population of San Francisco, which according to the State census of 1852 was 34,776, was estimated in 1853 to be from 50,000 to 60,000.

SAN JOSE

Pages 629-629

SAN JOSE, the capital of the republic of Costa Rica, in Central America, on the river Cartago, 248 miles W. by N. of Panama; N. Lat. 9° 46', W. Long. 84°. It is quite a modern town, and though the seat of the government, legislature, and law courts, and containing a cathedral and episcopal palace, has few remarkable buildings. There is here a large tobacco factory; and an active trade is carried on. Pop. 30,000.

SAN JUAN DE LA FRONTERA

SAN LUCAR

Pages 629-629

SAN LUCAR, a town of Spain in the province and 17 miles N. of Cadiz, in a bare, sandy, undulating country, on the left bank of the Guadalquivir, not far from its mouth. It stands partly on the flat bank of the river, and partly on the rising ground behind; its white glittering houses rising one above the other, up to an old Moorish castle on the summit. There are here 3 churches, 4 hospitals, one of them founded by Henry VIII. for English sailors, and the deserted buildings of several suppressed convents. The place is, however, dull and lifeless; having fallen off very much from its ancient commercial importance. It is now chiefly dependent on the wine trade, and is the mart of the inferior vintages sent to England as sherry. Many of the people are also employed in agriculture and fishing. The climate is hot, but not unhealthy. It was from San Lucar, in 1519, that the first voyage round the globe was begun by Magellan, who never returned, having been slain by the savages of the Philippines. Pop. 16,861.

SAN LUSSURGULI, a town of the Island of Sardinia, in the division of Sassari, in a valley inclosed by mountains, 8 miles W.S.W. of Cagliari. Its narrow winding streets are lined with good houses; and there are several churches, a convent, and a school. Woollen and linen cloth are manufactured; and there is some trade in cattle, wool, &c.
