Dollenstein, near Kahla, the loftiest point in the country, does not exceed 1000 feet in height. The principal river in this part is the Saale, an affluent of the Elbe, which receives here the Orla and the Roda; the eastern part of the duchy being watered by the Pleise, which afterwards unites with the Saale. The climate is temperate, pleasant, and healthy. There are mineral springs at Ronneburg and other places. With the exception of minerals, which are few, Saxe-Altenburg has all the ordinary natural productions. Agriculture is, especially in the eastern part, carried on with diligence and success. The quantity of arable land in the country is 213,982 acres; of wood, 66,838; of meadows, 24,200; of gardens, 10,822; and of pasture land, 7030. The quantity of corn raised is more than sufficient for domestic consumption. Pulse, potatoes, and other vegetables, are also grown. Cattle are raised in large numbers, and of a good breed; the horses and sheep are also excellent. The duchy contains 6200 horses; 56,000 horned cattle; 75,000 sheep; and 25,000 pigs. Deer and wild boars are found in the woods, and fish in the streams. Coal, building-stone, and porcelain-clay, are the most important minerals. Manufactures are not very extensively carried on in Altenburg: woollen, cotton, and linen cloth; wooden articles; beer, brandy, and vinegar, are among the articles produced; and there are also tanneries and dye-works. The trade is of some importance, and is facilitated by the good roads and railways. Corn, cattle, butter, cheese, wool, and timber, are among the principal exports. The educational establishments of the duchy include a gymnasium at Altenburg, with 10 teachers and 140 scholars, in 1854–5; a lyceum; normal seminary; a school of art and industry; 192 elementary schools, &c. The government is a limited monarchy; the dukedom is hereditary.

SAXE-COBURG-GOTHA

Pages 689-690

a small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Germany, comprising, besides several smaller portions, two separate districts, forming the duchies of Coburg and Gotha respectively, lying between N. Lat. 50° 8' and 51° 20'; E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 15' and 11° 14'. The duchy of Gotha, which forms the northern portion, is bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> on the N.; by Saxe-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a> on the E. and W.; by Saxe-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEININGEN">Meiningen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>-Cassel, Prussia, and Schwartzburg, on the S.; while that of Coburg is bounded on the W. and N. by Saxe-Meiningen; E. and S. by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> are as follows: | | Sq. miles | Pop. (1855) | |----------|-----------|-------------| | Coburg | 212 | 44,467 | | Gotha | 647 | 106,611 | | Total | 759 | 150,878 | The surface is in both the duchies partly occupied with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; that of Gotha lies on the northern slope of the Thuringian Forest, which extends along its south-western frontier; while the rest of this duchy consists of low, undulating, and very fertile <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The loftiest summits of the Thuringian chain are Schneeekopf, 3119 feet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; Beerberg, 3140 feet; and Inselsberg, 2909 feet. In the duchy of Coburg there are extensive forests, and many beautiful valleys among the hills. The slope here is towards the south; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> river is the Itz, which flows in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and falls into the Main. In Gotha, the Werra, an affluent of the Weser, takes its rise, and flows N.W.; and the Unstrut forms the eastern boundary, and flows northwards to join the Saale. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of arable land in the duchy is 1,139,819 acres; of wood, 600,569 acres; of meadows, 147,599 acres; of gardens, 31,766; and of waste land, 143,637 acres. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> is carried on with much care, and is the chief occupation of the people. Corn and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> are the crops most generally raised; also <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, potatoes, and other vegetables, are cultivated. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very rich and fertile in the valleys and plains; and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is throughout the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> healthy. In Coburg it is very mild; but in the mountainous parts of Gotha of a more inclement character. Pastoral employments are actively pursued by many of the inhabitants; the sheep especially are of an excellent breed, and the horses and cattle are not bad. There were, in 1852, 7063 horses; 56,207 horned cattle; 120,693 sheep; 18,266 goats; and 36,207 pigs. Fish abound in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and wild animals in the forests of the country. The German <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> infests the land in vast numbers. Among the minerals, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, coal, cobalt, and manganese, are worked; marble, alabaster, rock-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>-clay, &c., are also found. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, especially of the duchy of Gotha, are of some importance. The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, woollen, and cotton fabrics; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-making; the manufacture of iron, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>; of chemical products, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, beer, brandy, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, are extensively carried on; while much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, tar, pitch, &c., are prepared in the woods. The trade of the country is considerable. Among the exports are corn, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, salt, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, metallic and wooden wares, porcelain, marble, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, &c. There is also a considerable transit trade, as the duchy of Gotha is traversed by a line of railway which communicates with Leipzig on the one side, and with Frankfort on the other. The educational establishments include 3 gymnasia, a progymnasium, 2 normal seminaries, numerous industrial and other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and upwards of 300 elementary schools. The form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> in Saxe-Coburg-Gotha is monarchical. The highest office, which is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> line, is occupied by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, who exercises the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a>; and in the legislature is limited by a diet. Each of the duchies has a separate diet, that of Coburg consisting of 11, and that of Gotha of 19 members; but, besides these, there is one general diet for the whole state, to which the Coburg diet appoints 7, and that of Gotha 14 members. The elections to the separate diets take <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by means of electors equal in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> to the members to be chosen, each appointed by a certain district of the country. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of a diet is four years, and it must meet at least in the first and last of these, while not more than six months must intervene between two diets. The duke has the power of summoning, adjourning, and dissolving the diets. Under the upper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> at Jena, the judicial authority in the duchy is exercised by two colleges of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, beneath which there are several inferior courts. There is no established form of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; but all alike enjoy the protection of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. The duke, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> majority of his subjects, belong to the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>; while there are about 2300 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, and 1200 Jews, in the country. The annual revenue of Coburg for the financial <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> 1855–61 is estimated at L.34,725, and the annual expenditure (including L.5581 <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the debt) at L.34,312. In the administration of the public lands the annual receipts for 1855–61, were estimated at L.15,118, and the expenditure at L.10,488. As to the duchy of Gotha, the public revenue for the period 1858–61 was estimated at L.83,478 annually; and the expenditure (including L.13,303 interest on the debt) at L.83,913. The public debt amounts to L.157,346, including L.60,000 of paper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. The annual receipts of the public lands in this duchy are L.80,724, and the annual expenditure L.55,802. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> force of the country amounts to one regiment of 1860 men. Coburg, which, in the earliest times, was immediately dependent on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, came, in 1348, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a>, and through it, in 1428, to that of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>. By the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Leipzig, in 1485, it fell to the Ernestine line of the latter house; and, in 1542, was made a separate duchy under John Ernest, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>, John Frederick, who regained it in 1554, after his brother's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Meanwhile this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> had been deprived, in 1547, by the emperor of his electoral lands and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, but received as compensation several lands, among which was the present duchy of Gotha. Various and continually changing divisions of the country among the descendants of John Frederick I. took place, during which Coburg and Gotha, which then formed a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Weimar, were assigned now to one and now to another branch of the family. Gotha first became an independent state in 1640, under Duke Ernest the Pious; and was afterwards increased by the gradual addition of other lands, until it included all the territory of the Ernestine house, with the exception of Weimar. Ernest, however, died in 1675, leaving <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sons; who, after reigning jointly for five years, proceeded to a partition of the country, and founded seven new <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, viz., Gotha, Coburg, Meiningen, Römhild, Eisenberg, Hildburghausen, and Saalfeld. Of these the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was the first to expire, in 1699, when the district of Coburg was annexed to Saalfeld. Gotha obtained, in 1707, the possessions of the extinct line of Eisenberg; and, in 1710, only the four lines of Gotha, Meiningen, Hildburghausen, and Saalfeld, remained. Frederick II., grandson of Ernest the Pious, introduced the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of primogeniture into Gotha; and the duchy has not since been divided. His family, however, became extinct in 1823. Meanwhile the house of Saalfeld, which, in 1745, assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Coburg-Saalfeld, obtained several accessions of land at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>; and, in 1826, a new <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the country was adopted. Gotha was then joined to Coburg, while Saalfeld and other districts were transferred to Meiningen. The ducal family of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, formerly of Saalfeld, descending from the youngest son of Ernest the Pious, has been rendered illustrious by its connection with several of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> families of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The prince-consort of this country is the brother and heir-apparent of the reigning duke; the father of the present <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> is his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>; and another of his cousins is married to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> Philippe of France; while one of his uncles is king of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELGIUM">Belgium</a>. Important reforms in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> were introduced in 1846, and consequently no serious revolutionary outbreak took place in 1848.

SAXE-MEININGEN

Pages 690-690

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Germany, lying between N. Lat. 50° 13' and 50° 58'; E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 28' and 11° 25'; bounded on the N. by parts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>-Cassel, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, Gotha, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a>, and Altenburg; E. by Schwartzburg and Reuss; S. by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> and Coburg; and W. by Weimar. It has the form of a semi-circle <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> bow, curving towards the south; and its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> is 981 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The surface is throughout hilly, and in some parts mountainous. It is divided into the upper and the lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>; the former occupying the eastern <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the duchy, which is traversed by the range of the Thuringian Forest; the latter in the west, being occupied by the south-western slope of these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and by the eastern part of the Rhön range. About the middle, between the two, lies the principality of Hildburghausen; and to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> land that of Saalfeld; both of which are now included in the duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEININGEN">Meiningen</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> summits are Kieferle, in the Thuringian range, 2786 feet high; and Gebahre, in the Rhön mountains, 2378 feet high. The principal river in the duchy is the Werra, which is formed by the union of two small streams, and flows in a north-west <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The Saale crosses the north-east of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and the Milz, Steinach, and Itz, which all flow into the Main, take their rise in Saxe-Meiningen. There are several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in the country; and mineral <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> at Salzungen and Liebenstein. With the varying <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of the ground, the character of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> varies; in the lowland regions it is much milder than in the highland, where <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a> and snow sometimes occur as early as September. In many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions the territory of Meiningen is very rich. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of arable land in the country is about 243,700 acres; of wood, 224,900 acres; of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> land, 42,500 acres; of gardens and vineyards, 12,600 acres; and of waste land nearly 90,000 acres. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> is actively carried on, though not in all parts of the country, on account of its mountainous character. Besides wheat, which is cultivated chiefly in the lowland region, potatoes and other vegetables, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, &c., are raised. The forests furnish an important article of export; the amount of wood exported annually being more than 12,000,000 cubic feet. The live stock of the country in 1849 included 4060 horses, 68,464 horned cattle, 107,355 sheep, 19,673 goats, and 49,598 pigs. The mineral produce is also considerable. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">Iron</a>, pure and argentiferous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, cobalt, coal, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, sulphur, marble, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, are obtained; and the working of the various <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> employed, in 1822, 3820 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a> are actively carried on in the country. Iron is worked; glass and porcelain are made; woollen, cotton, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> fabrics are woven; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> is manufactured; <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a>, distilling, and various other branches of industry are carried on. The trade of the duchy is considerable. The principal exports are <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, which is generally floated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Werra; iron, hardware, glass, porcelain, paper, &c., which are conveyed to various countries, especially to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the people is well attended to in Saxe-Meiningen. There were, in 1853, 234 elementary <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, 2 gymnasia, a normal school, and various other institutions. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the state is monarchical; at the head of it stands the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, who exercises the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a>; and is limited in his legislative functions by a diet. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> consists of 24 deputies; two appointed by the duke, six by the landowners, eight by the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and eight by those of the country. The duke, and the majority of the people, belong to the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and there are only about 1000 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, 1550 Jews, and 80 Mennonites. The judicial establishments consist of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> at Hildburghausen, subordinate to that of Jena, and several inferior tribunals. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> consists of a regiment of infantry, 1726 strong. For the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> 1856-59, the annual public revenue is estimated at L.137,026, and the expenditure at L.154,993. The amount of debt on the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1857 was L.302,507. Pop. (1857) 165,662. The present ducal family of Meiningen is descended from Bernhard, the third son of Ernest the Pious, of Gotha, who received, in the partition of 1680, the duchy of Meiningen, comprising the greater part of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Henneberg, which had fallen, in 1583, to the Saxon states. When the line of Coburg became extinct in 1699, Meiningen entered into a protracted contest with Gotha, Hildburghausen, and Saalfeld, for the possession of its territories; which were at last, in 1723, adjudged by the Aulic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> to Meiningen, Hildburghausen, and Saalfeld, in equal portions. Similar disputes arose on the extinction, in 1710, of the line of Römhild, part of whose possessions were adjudged, in 1714, to Meiningen. The most important changes of territory in subsequent times occurred in 1826. In the partition which then took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, Meiningen received nearly the whole duchy of Hildburghausen, whose duke obtained Altenburg in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>; the principality of Saalfeld, and other districts, from Coburg; from Gotha, the portion of Römhild which had previously belonged to that duchy; and from Altenburg some small districts. Since that period no alterations of territory have taken place.

SAXE-WEIMAR-EISENACH

Pages 690-691

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Germany, lying between N. Lat. 50° 25' and 51° 27'; E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 24' and 11° 49', consists of three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> portions, besides other smaller districts. The most westerly of these, the principality of Eisenach, is bounded on the N. by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; E. by Saxo-Coburg-Gotha and Saxo-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEININGEN">Meiningen</a>; S. by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>; and W. by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>-Cassel; the central and largest portion, on the W., N., and N.E. by Prussia; S.W. and S. by Altenburg and Schwartzburg; and the third portion lies between the larger <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Reuss on the S., and Altenburg, with a smaller part of Reuss, on the N.; and between <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> on the E., and Schwartzburg on the W. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the various parts are as follows: | Principality | Circles | Sq. miles | Pop. (1855) | |--------------|---------|-----------|-------------| | Eisenach | Eisenach | 666 | 80,551 | | <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a> | Weimar | 691 | 135,178 | | | Neustadt| 241 | 48,023 | | Total | | 1,398 | 283,755 | The surface is generally undulating; and in some parts, especially in Eisenach, rises into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; there are also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> tracts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> along the banks of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. In a small separate portion of the grand duchy, the district of Ilmenau, near the S.E. extremity of the Thuringian Forest, rises Hinkelstein, the highest summit in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to the height of nearly 2700 feet. Eisenach is occupied in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Thuringian Mountains, more than 1300 feet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and in the south by those of Rhön, whose highest point, that of Ellenbogenberg, has an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of about 2500 feet. The circle of Neustadt is traversed by several offsets of the Erz Mountains, stretching from S.E. to N.W. Among the rivers which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> the grand duchy is the Saale, traversing the E. of Weimar, and receiving the Ilm, which rises in Ilmenau, and traverses the circle of Weimar. The Saale also receives the Elster and the Orla, which are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> rivers in the circle of Neustadt. The principality of Eisenach is watered by the Werra, and by its affluents, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FULDA">Fulda</a>, Ulster, Suhl, and Orsel. In most parts of the country the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is temperate, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> pure and healthy. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">Cold</a> and raw <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> frequently occurs in the mountainous regions; while in the valley of the Saale it is extremely pleasant. In spite of many difficulties which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> offers to the cultivator, farming is carried on with much diligence and success. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of corn raised frequently exceeds the demand; potatoes, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, hops; and on the banks of the Saale, vines are also grown. A valuable article of produce is <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>. The amount of arable land in the country is about 495,300 acres; of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> land, 81,400 acres; of gardens and vineyards, 18,750 acres; and of forests, 225,250 acres. Among the live stock of the country, the chief are sheep, of a good breed, especially in the circle of Weimar, and horned cattle, in those of Neustadt and Eisenach. In all, the grand duchy contains more than 12,000 horses, 112,000 horned cattle, 236,000 sheep, 60,000 swine, and 13,000 goats. Of the mineral produce of the land, coal, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, cobalt, and marble, are the most important <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The chief <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of the country are those of woollen, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and cotton cloth; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, and the working of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. The greatest amount of manufacturing industry exists in the circle of Eisenach, though Neustadt is the principal seat of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>-manufacture. Wool and grain form the staple of a trade which is actively carried on. The chief of the educational establishments in the grand duchy is the University of Jena, which belongs equally to the other Saxon duchies. (See JENA.) Besides this there are 2 gymnasia, 2 normal seminaries, and, in addition to various other establishments, 460 elementary <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> is a limited <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> line. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a> is in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the grand <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>, and the legislative is shared with a diet, consisting of 31 deputies; of whom 21 are elected by universal suffrage, 4 by those who possess landed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the annual value of L.145, 5 by those who have a revenue of the same amount from other sources, and 1 by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> who possess estates. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a> is administered by an upper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> at Jena, whose authority extends over all the Saxon duchies, the principalities of Reuss and Schwartzburg, and the duchy of Anhalt-Dessan-Cöthen. Beneath this there is an appeal court at Eisenach, and various subordinate tribunals. The grand duke, and the majority of his subjects, belong to the Evangelical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>; but there are also about 10,000 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, and 1430 Jews, in the country. For the financial <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, 1857-59, the annual revenue of the state was estimated at L.224,757, and the expenditure at L.223,902; while the public debt, Jan. 1, 1855, amounted to L.916,259. The territories of this state, which formerly belonged to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> of Saxony, fell to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of the Ernestine line at the partition in 1485. After the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of John Frederick I. in 1547, numerous divisions took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the different branches of the family; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of primogeniture having been only introduced at a later period among these states. At the first of these divisions, in 1566, Weimar, with Gotha for its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, was given to John Frederick II., eldest son of the deposed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a>; and the rest of the country, under the name of Thuringia, to John William, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son. The latter, however, after his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> had, by attempting to regain the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, incurred the fate of his father, obtained possession of Weimar, leaving Coburg and Eisenach to his two nephews, whose families became extinct in 1638. John William left two sons, the elder of whom founded the old Altenburg line; while the younger, John, had eleven sons, among whom were William, the immediate ancestor of the present family of Weimar, and Ernest, of all the other ducal houses. After this period the line of Weimar was not mixed up in the various divisions that took place among the other duchies, though it was itself once more subdivided, in 1672, into Weimar, Eisenach, and Jena. But these were reunited by the extinction of the line of Jena in 1690, and of that of Eisenach in 1741; while, in 1719, the right of primogeniture was introduced, which put an end to all further subdivisions. The most celebrated duke of Saxo-Weimar, in recent times, was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Augustus (1758-1828), who acted the part of a Macceans towards the science, art, and literature of Germany, took part in the contest against <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a>, and received at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, in 1815, along with the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of grand duke, several additions to his dominions.

SAXO

Pages 691-692
or as he is generally called, Saxo Grammaticus, or the Grammarian, was descended from an illustrious Danish family, and was born about the middle of the twelfth century. Stephens, in his edition of Saxo Grammaticus, printed at Sorø, indubitably proves that he must have been alive in 1156; but he cannot ascertain the exact place and time of his birth. On account of his uncommon learning, Saxo was distinguished by the name of Grammaticus. He was provost of the cathedral church of Roskild, and warmly patronized by the learned and warlike Absalon, the celebrated archbishop of Lund, at whose instigation he wrote the History of Denmark. His epitaph, which is a dry panegyric in bad Latin verses, gives no account of the era of his death, which happened, according to Stephens, in 1204. His history, consisting of sixteen books, begins from the earliest account of the Danish annals, and concludes with the year 1186. It bears the title, Historia Regum Heronamque Danorum, and first gives the history of King Hamlet. According to the opinion of an accurate writer, the first part, which relates to the origin of the Danes, and the reigns of the ancient kings, is full of fables; but the eight last books, and particularly those which regard the events of his own times, deserve the utmost credit. He wrote in Latin; and the style, if we consider the barbarous age in which he flourished, is in general extremely elegant, but rather too poetical for history. Mallet, in his *Histoire de Danemark* (vol. i., p. 182), says that "Sperling, a writer of great erudition, has proved, in contradiction to the assertions of Stephens and others, that Saxo Grammaticus was secretary to Absalon, and that the Saxo, provost of Roskild, was another person, and lived earlier."

SAXONY

Pages 692-695

a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Germany, lying between N. Lat. 50° 10' and 51° 23', E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 23' and 14° 34'; bounded on the N. and N.E. by the Prussian provinces of Saxony and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, S.E. and S. by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and W. by Reuss, Saxe-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEIMAR">Weimar</a>, Saxe-Altenburg, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. Its form is nearly triangular; its length from N.E. to S.W. about 150 miles, breadth about 75; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, 5760 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The northern <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the kingdom is for the most part a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> an undulating <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but on the south it is very mountainous. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mountain ranges are the Erzgebirge, extending along the Bohemian frontier, and reaching their highest elevation in the Fichtelberg, 3818 feet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; the Lusatian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, forming a continuation of the former range on the E. of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, with Lausche, 2530 feet high; and the Elbe sandstone range, extending along both sides of the Elbe, from Dresden to Bohemia. This last mountainous district, usually denominated Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, has peculiar charms for the lovers of picturesque scenery. It is about 28 miles in length and 23 in breadth, displaying deep chasms bordered by perpendicular rocks, some naked, and others clothed with every variety of trees. Rapid streams pour from declivities, forming cascades in some parts, and in others in deep vales, meandering through verdant meadows, without their entrance or their egress being discoverable by the observer from the precipices which enclose them. Through this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of mountains the River Elbe has worn itself a passage by a most tortuous course, and washes the bases of rocks, in some parts of nearly 1000 feet in perpendicular height. From the surface of this mountain-plain rise pinnacles of rocks, on which castles in the feudal times were erected, some of the ruins of which add to the romantic <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of the prospect; whilst others, such as Königstein, have had applied to them all the arts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> fortification, and are the most impregnable fortresses in the Saxon dominions. Königstein has on its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a> strong walls, surrounding buildings in which the treasures of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> are secured in times of danger. Few spots in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> create greater <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the geologist, the botanist, or the lover of picturesque scenery, than this portion of the country so appropriately denominated Saxon Switzerland. The principal river of Saxony, and that to which almost all the others contribute their streams, though not till it has left this kingdom, is the Elbe. It enters from Bohemia, and is navigable through the whole of its Saxon course. The other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Elster, which rises in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LUSATIA">Lusatia</a>, and soon enters the Prussian territory; and the Spree, which comes out of Bohemia, divides itself into two branches near Bautzen, and then passes into Prussia. These rivers <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the Elbe on its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a>. On the left bank it receives the Mulde, which is formed by the confluence of the Zwickau or western, and the Freiberg or eastern Mulde, both rising in the Erzgebirge, and flows northwards till it joins the Elbe at Dessau. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Elster rises in the Voigtländ, or south-western portion of the Erzgebirge, with many curvatures reaches the suburbs of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Leipzig, and, receiving there the small river Pleisse, falls into the Saale, and is ultimately lost in the Elbe above <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a>. The only river that does not run to the Elbe is the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEISSE">Neisse</a>, which rises in the eastern corner of the kingdom, and, passing into Silesia, at length empties itself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ODER">Oder</a>. There are no considerable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> in Saxony, nor any <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, except such as are used in the mining districts for conveying the ore to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>. As compared with most parts of Germany, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> of Saxony is much advanced. Wherever the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is capable of cultivation it is worked with diligence; and the more hilly and poorer soils have a good herbage, and yield pasture to numerous flocks and herds. The sides of the mountains towards the Elbe, from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIRNA">Pirna</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a>, are covered with vines which yield both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> and white wine, to the amount of 145,320 gallons in 1855. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of arable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> in the kingdom is estimated at 1,839,000 acres, of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> land at 413,000 acres, of gardens and vineyards at 45,000 acres, and of forests at 1,131,000 acres. The arable land is chiefly cultivated on a three-course system, though in the Voigtländ there are generally four courses. Rye, wheat, barley, and oats are the crops most generally raised. Notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> paid to farming, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> excellence of the soil in several parts, there is not produced more than enough of grain to supply the wants of the dense <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>. Peas, beans, lentils, and vetches are grown. The culture of potatoes is very extensive, and they form almost exclusively the food of the labouring classes in the mountainous districts. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, wood, hops, and chicory, are grown in some parts of the kingdom, but none of them to the extent which the consumption of the country requires. The forests of Saxony form one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> sources of wealth to the country. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">Timber</a> of excellent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is obtained from them to the amount of more than 62,000,000 cubic feet annually. Pastoral occupations afford employment to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the inhabitants. The cattle are good, especially in the Voigtländ and Erzgebirge, where <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> are produced. As to the rearing of sheep, generally of a good breed, this country occupies the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in Germany; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> and pigs are also numerous. There were, in 1853, 94,925 horses, 610,836 horned cattle, 485,147 sheep, 74,726 goats, and 124,158 pigs. The wild animals of the country are at present of little importance. Saxony abounds in minerals, and the ore is tolerably rich; which, added to superior skill and economy in working the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> and separating the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, makes them very beneficial to the crown, to whom the greater portion of them belong. In 1854 there were in operation 362 mines in all, besides a large number of smelting-houses. The value of the silver obtained in 1850 was £206,176; and the total value of the mineral produce about £428,000. Besides silver, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, tin, coal, sandstone, sulphur, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and many other minerals, are found in the kingdom. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">Salt</a>, however, is entirely absent, and has to be imported from Prussian Saxony. In no part of the continent has manufacturing industry been carried to so great an extent, or occupied so large a proportion of the population, as in Saxony. It is in the mountainous regions of Lusatia and the Erzgebirge that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are most extensively carried on; and in these regions there are not only many manufacturing <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, but villages, which in size, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of business, surpass many towns. The first manufacturing town of the country is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHEMNITZ">Chemnitz</a>. More than the half of the people are engaged in manufactures. The annual value of the whole produce of Saxon industry is estimated at thirteen millions <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. It would include almost the whole catalogue of European manufactures to enumerate the respective kinds of goods made in Saxony. Woollens, linens, cottons, and silks for clothing; iron, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and copper wares; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, earthenware, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, musical instruments, and turnery <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; various chemical and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> preparations; clocks, watches, swords, guns, and pistols, are all comprehended in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> of Saxon manufactures. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of a country whose inhabitants are chiefly Saxony, occupied in manufactures, and produce an insufficiency of food for their own consumption, must necessarily be extensive. The trade of Saxony chiefly centres in the city of Leipzig, where, at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the three annual <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, the greater part of the manufactures are disposed of, and contracts are made for such foreign commodities as the supply of the country demands. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> in Saxony are generally good, and these, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RAILWAYS">railways</a>, of which there were in 1856 nearly 400 miles in operation, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of the Elbe, greatly facilitate the trade of the country. Saxony exports sheep's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, fine woollen goods, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and thread <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, yarn and worsted, ironmongery, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a>, and braziers, and also books. It receives in return corn, wine, salt, colonial wares, &c. The annual excess in value of the exports over the imports of Saxony is above L700,000; and the share of the kingdom in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NET">net</a> receipts of the German Zollverein amounted in 1855 to L318,976. The quantities of the principal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> exported and imported in 1855 are exhibited in the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a>: | Principal Articles | Import | Export | Transit | |--------------------|--------|--------|---------| | Books | 9,404 | 12,059 | 672 | | Cattle | (head) | 74,686 | 8,044 | | Coal | (cwt.) | 7,734 | 15,621 | | Copper and brass | | 9,693 | 7,264 | 1,242 | | Cotton pulps, seeds, berries (bushes) | 1,727,105 | 387,275 | | | Cotton and cotton stuffs (cwt.) | 260,628 | 150,856 | 162,094 | | Drugs, colours, &c.| | 203,841 | 126,929 | 139,684 | | Glass and glass ware | | 8,309 | 262,386 | 792 | | Grocery, &c. | | 322,779 | 83,305 | 278,311 | | Hardware | | 401 | 5,712 | 3,824 | | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">Hides</a>, &c. | | 33,301 | 8,228 | 2,448 | | Iron and <a class="xref" 2,917 | 3,863 | 595 | | <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SILK">Silk</a> and silk fabrics | | 3,569 | 5,122 | 3,887 | | Tallow and stearine| | 2,627 | 306 | 2,329 | | Tar, pitch, &c. | | 3,400 | 761 | 456 | | Tin and tin wares | | 1,353 | 116 | 966 | | Wood and wooden fabrics | 19,937 | 10,475 | 982 | | Wool and woollens | | 87,944 | 30,921 | 22,902 | The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> in the Saxon Albertine line, and, in failure of that, in the Ernestine or Saxe-Weimar branch of the family. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> enjoys the whole <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a>, confirms pardons, bestows commissions, nominates the supreme judges, and enjoys the power of making peace and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and of concluding all treaties. In making new laws, and in imposing new taxes, the states have the right to be consulted. The legislative body is a diet composed of two chambers, which meet at the same time, and possess equal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges. The first chamber includes, besides the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> from the University of Leipzig, one of the Evangelical and one of the Roman Catholic clergy, the supreme magistrates of Dresden, Leipzig, and other towns, &c. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> chamber there are twenty deputies from the possessors of manors, twenty-five from the towns, twenty-five from the country, and five representing the manufacturing and commercial interests. When the king pleases these states are convoked; but they must hold an ordinary meeting at least once every three years, and an extraordinary one on each change of ministry. The administration is conducted by a cabinet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, under which, through the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy council</a>, orders are communicated to the departments of finance, war, domains, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, and foreign affairs. According to the budget for 1858-60, the income and expenditure each amounted to L1,873,048; and the public debt at the end of 1857 was L12,264,802. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> force of Saxony is composed of the following troops: - Infantry of the line, forming 4 regiments: 15,748 - Chasseurs: 4,605 - Cavalry: 3,208 - <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a>: 2,430 - Commanding officers: 15 Total (exclusive of the reserve): 25,406 The whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINGENT">contingent</a> of Saxony to the German confederation is 18,000 men. Although the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family professes the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, the most of the people belong to the Lutheran <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>. In 1855 the number of Lutherans was 1,995,891; of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, 36,730; of the Reformed Church, 3602; of German Catholics, 1753; and of Jews, 1200. Toleration is extended to all sects recognised by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and these are the Lutheran, Reformed, Roman, Greek, and German Catholic Churches; but over all alike the civil government exercises the supreme <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> power. The educational institutions comprise the University of Leipzig, and in the endowed classical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of Meissen and Grimma, as well as in 11 gymnasia, 9 normal seminaries, 1892 elementary schools, and various other institutions. Both the higher and lower kinds of schools are well managed, and popular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> is widely spread throughout the country; so that in intellectual culture Saxony stands in the foremost rank among the nations of Europe. The fine arts have been cultivated with considerable success, and both statuary and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> receive valuable assistance from the fine productions which are contained in the collections of Dresden. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Saxony is Dresden and the country is divided into four circles, as follows: | Circle | Sq. Miles | Pop. (1855) | |--------------|-----------|-------------| | Dresden | 1,669 | 528,714 | | Leipzig | 1,338 | 454,262 | | Zwicken | 1,785 | 759,328 | | Bautzen | 968 | 295,771 | | Total | 5,700 | 2,039,075 | The early <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Saxon people is involved in considerable obscurity. According to the most <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> traditions of the people, they are represented as being the aboriginal inhabitants of the wide forests of their own country, living by agriculture and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>. As the population gradually increased, and became too great for the country, colonies were sent out from time to time. These settled on the coasts of the Cimbrian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, where they pursued a different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> from the inland tribes,—devoting themselves to commerce, and partly also to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PIRACY">piracy</a>. They rendered themselves so terrible to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> by their devastations that, in the reign of Theodosius, a Saxon frontier, guarded by Roman armies, was established along the shores of the German Ocean. It was from these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> Saxons that the bands came over to colonize Great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. After the ecclesiastical council at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a> in 774, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a> began a long and bloody war against the Saxons. He made repeated invasions into their country, in which he was almost uniformly successful; but as soon as his back was turned the enemy was again in arms. The result of the war was that, in 804, a great part of the Saxons were compelled to adopt Christianity, and submit to the power of the Franks. They were then governed by counts, generally of Frank origin, who were afterwards raised to the rank of dukes. Of these the most celebrated is Henry the Fowler (912-936), who was elected German <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, the first of the Saxon family who wore that crown. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> at that time did not correspond with the present Saxony, but with Westphalia, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>. The nucleus of the present kingdom of Saxony was formed by the erection in 926, by Henry the Fowler, of the margraviate of Meissen, comprising the country between the Elbe, the Saale, and the Erzgebirge, as a bul- <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> against the Slavonian tribes beyond. In 1139 the office of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MARGRAVE">margrave</a> became hereditary in the family of Wettin, who added to the territory of Meissen their own possessions in Thuringia, Saxony, Sambia, &c. Meanwhile the Duchy of Saxony, afterwards raised to an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a>, passed into the Ascanian family, the last <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of which, Albert III., died in 1422. As he left no issue, numerous claimants appeared for his land and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; but the Emperor Sigismund conferred them, in 1423, on Frederick the Quarrelsome, Margrave of Meissen, on account of the services he had rendered to the empire in the war against the Hussites. The territory of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Wettin had by this time extended far beyond its original limits, and stretched from the Werra to the Oder, and from the Erzgebirge to the Harz Mountains. The accession of Frederick to Saxony gave him little additional territory, but conferred much importance, by raising him to the second <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the temporal electors. Thus the name of the purest in blood of all the German tribes, passed over to a different people; and that of Saxony came to designate what had been formerly known as the margraviate of Meissen. The country had been very much improved by the discovery of its great mineral wealth, which led to the clearing of the immense forests; but in the beginning of the fifteenth century great devastations were caused by the incursions of the Hussite troops from Bohemia. Under the wise and energetic rule of Frederick the Quarrelsome, the University of Leipzig, an offshoot from that of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, was founded in 1409. Frederick was succeeded in 1428 by his son of the same name, surnamed the Gentle, who died in 1464, leaving two sons, Ernest and Albert, from whom the Ernestine and Albertine families of Saxony are descended. For some time they reigned conjointly; but in 1485 proceeded to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the country. Ernest, the elder of the two, obtained, along with the electorate and the territory attached to that office, the greater part of Thuringia, the Vogtland, and the district of Coburg; and Albert, the ancient Meissen, and the rest of Thuringia. The successors of Ernest in the electorate did good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the cause of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and freedom in supporting the rise of the Reformation. Frederick III. (1486–1525), founded the University of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WITTENBERG">Wittenberg</a>, and afforded his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, who was made professor there. John the Constant (1525–32) stood at the head of the protesting princes at the Diet of Spires in 1529; and John Frederick the Magnanimous (1532–47) took the lead against <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. in the Schmalkaldic war; and was defeated and taken prisoner in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Mühlberg in 1547. For this <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of rebellion he was deprived by the emperor of his electoral dignity and lands; and these were conferred on his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> Maurice, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Saxony. While the Ernestine branch of the family were thus contending in favour of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and protestantism, Albert and his immediate successor, who possessed the present kingdom of Saxony, were exerting their power on the opposite side. The former, in 1488, led an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, and delivered from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> Maximilian, king of the Romans, for which service he was appointed, in 1495, hereditary viceroy in Friesland, and general of the imperial army. He died, however, in 1500, in a vain attempt to subdue the Frisians; and his son George, who succeeded to the duchy, and in 1504 obtained Friesland from his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Henry, being equally unsuccessful in his efforts, gave up this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in 1515 to the Archduke of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> for 20,000 gulden about (£200,000). George strongly opposed the progress of the Reformation, and attempted to exclude, by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a>, any Protestant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> from the succession; but dying in 1539, leaving his will unsigned, he was succeeded by his brother Henry, a Lutheran, who introduced the reformed religion into the country. His son Maurice, who became duke in 1541 and elector in 1548, though he adhered to Charles V. in the Schmalkaldic war, afterwards opposed and put an end to the despotic designs of that emperor; and by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Passau in 1551, obtained for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> the free <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their religion. Maurice's brother and successor, August (1553–86), assisted in bringing about the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> peace of Augsburg in 1555, by which the Protestants obtained equal rights with the Roman Catholics, and also did much for the improvement of the laws and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of Saxony. Various additional districts were added to the electorate in this reign. The reigns of Christian I. (1586–91) and Christian II. (1591–1611) were distinguished only for religious disputes; but that of John George I., the brother and successor of the latter, includes the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the Thirty Years' War, in which he played no very illustrious part. He refused the Bohemian crown, which was offered to him, and not only advised the elector of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a> to do the same, but refused to afford him any assistance. He remained on the emperor's side till the arrival of Gustavus Adolphus; and after his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> made terms with the emperor at Prague in 1635, by which he obtained part of the see of Magdeburg, and the two Lusatian margraviates. His eldest son, John George II., succeeded in 1666; while the younger sons, August, Christian, and Maurice founded the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of Wessenfels, Merseburg, and Zeitz, which became extinct in 1746, 1738, and 1718, respectively. John George III. (1680–91), the son and successor of the last elector, distinguished himself by the assistance he gave to the emperor against the Turks in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and against France on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. After the short reign of John George IV., Frederick August I., surnamed the Strong, succeeded in 1691; and, in order to obtain the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a> crown of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, went over, in 1697, to the Roman Catholic Church. By this increase of power and territory, however, he involved himself in a war with the greatest soldier of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Charles XII. of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in which Saxony was invaded by the Swede, and suffered the loss of an immense amount of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and blood. Frederick August II., who succeeded his father in 1733, was also elected King of Poland. During this reign, as in the preceding, the wars and extravagance of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> reduced Saxony to the lowest pitch of misery. In the war of the Austrian succession, Frederick August took part with France and Prussia against Austria; but in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> Years' War he placed himself on the imperial side. In the latter contest Saxony was devastated alike by friend and foe, and was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of many of the victories of Frederick the Great. The wretched state of the country began to be ameliorated in the long reign of Frederick August III., who obtained the electorate in 1763 at the age of thirteen, and ruled at first under the guardianship of his uncle Xaver. A system of strict economy, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and mildness was introduced; the people were relieved from many burdensome imposts; the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of torture was abolished; and much was done for the material improvement of the country. A rising of the peasantry, which took place in 1790, was put <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> without loss of blood, and the grievances complained of were removed. In the wars which followed the French Revolution, Saxony took part with Prussia at first; but after the power of that kingdom was overthrown by the decisive battle of Jena in 1806, Frederick August made peace with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a>, and was made, with the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of king, a member of the Rhenish confederacy. By the peace of Tilsit in the following year he obtained several accessions of territory, and the sovereignty over the newly erected <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-duchy of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a>. During this time of his prosperity the monarch acted a very upright and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> part, in not taking advantage of his power to enrich himself at the expense of the surrounding small states, as he might easily have done. But a great reverse of fortune befell him after Saxony was treated as a conquered country; the king was kept in confinement for some time; and a partition of the kingdom was effected by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">Congress</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, whereby, besides the loss of the duchy of Warsaw, an area of 791 square miles, with a population of 845,218, was ceded to Prussia, to make up to that kingdom for its part of Poland, which Russia obtained. Notwithstanding this spoliation of more than half its territory, Saxony has since risen to a more flourishing and prosperous condition than ever. Frederick August I., (as king) died in 1827, having deservedly obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">Just</a>; and was succeeded by his brother Anthony, who carried on the various <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> which his predecessor had begun in the later years of his reign. Still the people suffered under many grievances, and had as yet very little share in the legislative power. The outbreaks which took place in 1830 in Dresden and Leipzig did not indeed cause any serious disturbance; but they led to the introduction of a new constitution in the following year. On the death of the king in 1836, his nephew, Frederick August II., who had been regent since 1830, ascended the throne. The constitutional system now established did not succeed altogether in the best possible way. A powerful party was formed in opposition to the government; and in the year 1843 violent contests began, in which the opposition gradually gained the upper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The chief <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in dispute were the freedom of the press and the publicity of judicial proceedings. The government followed the fatal policy of delaying to yield as long as possible, so that the concessions which would in 1843 have been received with universal joy, were granted in 1846 without any effect. An attack was made in Leipzig in 1845 upon Prince John, the heir-apparent; and having been put down by the military, led to a still more violent opposition on the part of the popular party. The ministry, however, still held their ground during the stormy session of 1845-6; but were at last compelled to resign in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1848, when a liberal cabinet was formed. Various changes were introduced in the following year, especially with regard to the mode of electing the legislature, but these were not of long continuance; and the diet of 1852, elected after the old manner, restored the constitution almost entirely as it was before 1848. Falkenstein, who was one of the ministry previous to 1848, and resigned in that year, is now again in the cabinet, and has been since 1853. In 1854, the king was killed by an accident while travelling in the Tyrol, and was succeeded by his brother John, the present king. Saxony (Germ. Sachsen), a province of the Prussian monarchy, lying between 50° 55' and 53° 5 N. Lat., 9° 22' and 13° 21' E. Long.; bounded on the N.E. by the province of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, S. by the kingdom of Saxony and the Saxon duchies, W. and N.W. by Electoral <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, and Hanover. Area, 9760 square miles. It has several detached portions lying among the Saxon duchies, and encloses portions of these as well as the duchies of Anhalt and the principalities of Schwartzburg. It is for the most part a flat country, consisting of the land lying between the Thuringian Mountains in the S., the Harz Mountains in the W., and the Elbe in the E. and N. The Harz Mountains belong partly to this province, and within its limits is their highest summit, the Brocken, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a> peak 3508 feet high; and another called Konigsberg, which attains the height of 3100 feet, besides others of less elevation. To that part of the Thuringian mountain which is included in the province belongs the summit of Dolmar, 2100 feet high. The lower portions of the country are watered by the Elbe, which enters the province at its south-eastern extremity, and flows in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> course to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west, never very far from the borders of Brandenberg, which it touches in the lower part of its course. This river receives, either directly or indirectly, all the other streams of Saxony. The Saale flows northwards from the Thuringian Mountains into the Elbe; the Mulde, also an affluent of the Elbe, flows in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> further east, and nearly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the Saale; and the Unstrut flows from the west and joins the Saale. The whole of the soil of Saxony is not only very fertile, but exceedingly well cultivated; and it enjoys a mild and salubrious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. The extent of arable land in the province was, in 1852, 3,377,069 acres; of gardens, vineyards, &c., 70,487 acres; of meadows, 424,701 acres; of pasture land, 394,597 acres; of forests, 955,511 acres; and of waste land, 1,403,689 acres. Cattle, sheep, and horses are raised in great numbers in Saxony. There were in 1855, 152,485 horses; 502 mules and asses; 522,380 horned cattle; 1,938,945 sheep; 144,255 goats; and 332,490 pigs in the province. The mineral productions comprise silver, iron, lead, copper, coal, and salt. Marble, alabaster, granite, sandstone, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> clay are also found. Manufactures are actively carried on here, especially those of woollen and cotton cloth. Education is well provided for, and the proportion of the population who have enjoyed its advantages is higher here than in any other province of Prussia. There are in all 2872 public elementary schools, with 3794 teachers and 304,318 scholars; 66 intermediate schools for boys, with 11,480 scholars; 49 girls' schools, with 11,036 scholars; 11 normal seminaries; 4 progymnasia; and 21 gymnasia. Saxony contains also one university, that of Halie, with which the former one at Wittenberg has been united. The great majority of the inhabitants are of German <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>; 1,758,130 belong to the Evangelical Church, 118,064 to the Roman Catholic; 5 to the Greek Church, 16 are Mennonites, and 5320 Jews. Saxony is divided into three circles, as follows: | Square Miles | Pop. (1850) | |--------------|------------| | Magdeburg | 4453 | 727,052 | | Merseburg | 3999 | 781,947 | | <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ERFURT">Erfurt</a> | 1308 | 352,536 | | Total | 9760 | 1,881,535 | The greater part of this province till 1815, formed part of the kingdom of Saxony; but by the congress of Vienna it was annexed to Prussia.

SAY

Pages 695-696

Jean Baptiste, a French <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> economist, was born at Lyons on the 5th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1767, of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> commercial family of Protestant refugees. Say was originally designed for the family trade, but having always been of a meditative turn, he showed early a decided fondness for letters. In his youth he assisted Mirabeau and Claviere, and during the Reign of Terror he was one of the conductors of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECADE">Decade</a> Philosophique, the sole scientific and literary monument of that bloody <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Being requested to take <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the affairs of the tribunate by Bonaparte, then first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, he remained faithful to his political convictions; and when <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a> was subsequently raised to the empire, Say voted against it, and withdrew in 1804. He was for a time <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of taxes for the department of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALLIER">Allier</a>, but afterwards resigned this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> to popularize the science of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Smith and Quesnay. Say was not a discoverer in political economy, but was a very intelligent expounder of the principles of that science as originated by others. His distinguishing merit is that of a skilful exponent of truths and principles already known and fully established; and except in his inquiry relating to glut, he left the science of political economy exactly in the same state as he found it. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> on the 16th of November 1832. Say's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are—Traité d'Economie Politique, 2 vols., 1802; and 5 vols. in 1826, afterwards expanded into the Cours Complet d'Economie Politique Pratique, 6 vols., 1829; Catechisme d'Economie Politique, 1815, fifth edition, 1826.
